name: Zopiclone

tolerance.full: within a couple of weeks of daily use

toxicities: Potentially lethal when mixed with depressants like benzodiazepines, alcohol or opioids
summary: A nonbenzodiazepine sedative sleep aid (Z-drug), which can have hallucinogenic effects if taken while awake. Often causes users to have a metallic taste in the mouth for ~12h. Has been reported in some cases to cause certain users to black out, redose excessively and undertake dangerous activities such as driving.
saferUse: Treatment should be limited to the shortest useful duration, a single course no longer than 4 weeks including tapering. Both dependence and withdrawal reactions can occur even with short-term use at recommended doses.

Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants; the label reports additive CNS depression. Do not drive or operate machinery within 12 hours of taking zopiclone, and do not re-dose during the same night. Take it only when a full night's sleep (about 7-8 hours) is possible, because anterograde amnesia and complex sleep behaviours (sleep walking, sleep driving) have been reported.

CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir) raise zopiclone exposure; CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, St John's wort) lower it. The label says taking it together with CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided in the elderly.
metabolism: The main breakdown products are the N-oxide form, which is active in animals, and the N-desmethyl form, which is not. A lab study points to CYP3A4 as the main enzyme that makes both of them, with CYP2C8 also helping to make the N-desmethyl form. It is mostly cleared by being broken down: about 80% comes out in the urine as the free breakdown products, the N-oxide and N-desmethyl forms, and about 16% in the faeces.
